description.narrative:
The overall objective of this contribution is to strengthening the health system in Somalia by supporting the building and strengthening of essential public health functions.
The specific objective of the intervention is to:
1) Support the establishment of an independent National Institute for Health (NIH) in Somalia, and;
2) Strengthening the Health Management Information System (HMIS) in pilot locations across Somalia, as well as working towards the development of an integrated disease surveillance and response system in Somalia.

Denna insats skall ge finansiellt stöd till WHO Somalia och har som huvudsyfte att med WHO:s tekniska expertis stödja två andra svenska insatser som implementeras i Somalia, nämligen utvecklandet av en Somalisk Folkhälsomyndighet som sker i ett samarbete med den svenska folkhälsomyndigheten och att digitalisera Somalias hälsohanteringsinformationssystem som sker genom ett samarbete med Stockholms Universitet/SPIDER. Insatsen bygger dels på de arbetsplaner som WHO har överenskommit med folkhälsomyndigheten och med Stockholms universitet/SPIDER och dels på de arbetsbeskrivningar som tagits fram för de två experter som kommer stödja implementeringen.

This contribution will provide financial support to WHO Somalia to allow WHO to dedicate technical expertise two other Swedish initiatives implemented in Somalia and has as its main purpose to support two other Swedish initiatives implemented in Somalia, namely the development of a Somali Public Health Agency in collaboration with the Swedish Public Health Agency and to digitilize Somalia's health management information system which takes place through a collaboration with Stockholm University / SPIDER. The contribution is based on both the work plans that the WHO has agreed with the public health authority and with Stockholm University / SPIDER and also on the job descriptions prepared for the two experts WHO will provide to support the implementation.

This contribution provided financial support to WHO Somalia to allow WHO to dedicate technical expertise to two other Swedish initiatives implemented in Somalia, namely; National Institute of Health in collaboration with Public Health Agency of Sweden and the Digital Health inititive by Stockholm University/SPIDER.
Below are some examples of results that this collaboration has yielded over the last period:
In in 2024 it was decided to extend the contribution by 11 months up to May 2025 in order to align with the end date of the Public Health Agency / NIH contribution. The continuation has progressed as planned during 2024.
On a broader level, this contribution has supported the establishment of NIH and the strengthening of HMIS in Somalia. Besides the above-listed direct objectives, the contribution has resulted in that Sweden and WHO Somalia has been able to develop a close working relationship and networked together on a broad range of issues, such as health sector coordination, setting health sector priorities. The Sida Programme Manager has also visited WHO Somalia office and gone on field trips in Mogadishu to visit health facilities and hospitals supported by WHO.
Below are some examples of results from previous years:
Supporting the establishment of the NIH Somalia
The National Institute of Health (NIH), which was established in 2013 by the Federal Ministry of Health & Human Services, was designated as the national focal point for International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005 and therefore spearheads the implementation of the National Action Plan for Health Security. In 2021, through a ministerial directive, the National Institute of Health was assigned several functions including surveillance; national public health laboratories; human resources capacity development; health research; and public health emergency operations centres. To fulfil its responsibilities, and with support of the Public Health Agency of Sweden and WHO, the National Institute of Health developed a 3-year (2021-2023) strategic plan for strengthening public health system in the country 20212023. The plan was developed through a consultative workshop and has been implemented gradually since then. The Ministry of Health and Human Services, Federal Government of Somalia (FMOH), PHAS and WHO has continued to work together closely in line with this work plan and to hold regular (quarterly) meetings in order to revise the plan (as needed), assess implementation progress and add other critical activities which may arise. Furthermore, as part of this plan, WHO ihas been supporting the International Health Regulations (IHR), surveillance, laboratory, Public Health Emergency Operations Centres (PHEOC), research and human resources development components. Indeed, this plan has been fully supported by PHAS, especially in the areas of surveillance and research. In fact, there is a Swedish university already working with the NIH on research activities towards publication in peer reviewed medical journals.
Frontline Field Epidemiology Training Programme (FETP-Frontline)
To address Somalias limited capacity to detect and respond to health emergencies, WHO, PHAS, the United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (Af-CDC), and the Africa Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET), amongst other partners, supported the NIH in establishing the FETP-Frontline in August 2021 a three-month on-the-job training that covers the critical skills needed to conduct surveillance and response activities effectively at the local level, with a focus on improving disease detection, reporting and response, as well as developing the public health workforce in a country. So far, Three cohorts of the FETP-Frontline have been completed with 71 graduates (including 10 women), who are already contributing to disease surveillance and reporting in their communities, and additional cohorts are already underway.
First public health research conference laying the foundation for health research
The COVID-19 pandemic has accentuated the importance of health research in finding solutions to health challenges, which in part led the NIH and FMOH to convene the first public health research conference in Garowe, Somalia, from 30 January 1 February 2022. This conference, which was a milestone for research in Somalia, brought together 200 national and international researchers to present 50 research abstracts (7 of whom were women) that showcased new evidence and best practices in public health in Somalia. In addition, 12 panel presentations were held, which stimulated discussions on policy development and action in Somalia. The conference aimed to provide health researchers, academics and health care practitioners with the opportunity to present their ongoing research projects and share the successes, challenges and the gaps that their studies have identified.
Research prioritization workshop
Public health research prioritization is an integral component of public health system that has been carried out to effectively allocate limited health research resources, increase research value and decrease research wastage. In Somalia, despite the gains made through investments of the public health system in the past two decades, little attention has been given to building a national public health research system and production of knowledge relevant to the country. Moreover, no nationally unified public health research agenda exists in Somalia.
To overcome this gap following the research conference conducted in Garowe, the NIH, with support of the WHO, convened the first ever public health research prioritization workshop in Mogadishu from 9 10 March 2022. Attended by 60 health researchers from the public and private health sectors, academia, development partners and humanitarian agencies, the overall aim of this workshop was to reduce and achieve consensus from amongst 231 research questions proposed by public health researchers in Somalia, under four thematic areas: health system and social determinants; communicable diseases; non-communicable diseases; and reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health and nutrition. The participants prioritized 10 research questions under each thematic area, which produced a total of 40 public health research priorities. From these 40 public health research priorities, the highest ranking 10 public health research questions for the country were identified.
Integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) strategy for Somalia
In 2020, the FMOH and NIH made a strategic decision to develop and implement an integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) strategy for Somalia. Since then, and particularly during 2021, WHO and PHAS have supported the FMOH and NIH to establish IDSR, whereby the following milestones have been achieved:
- A functional technical working group coordination structure for IDSR implementation was established;
- A three-year operational plan for IDSR implementation was developed and costed;
- Technical guidelines (i.e. standard tools and SOPs) for IDSR implementation were developed and endorsed by the Minister of the FMOH;
- Training materials for supporting the roll-out of IDSR were developed;
- An Information Technology (IT) platform for supporting IDSR implementation (DHIS2-tracker) was developed and validated;
- A plan for rolling-out IDSR implementation was developed.
Public health emergency operations centres (PHEOC)
WHO is supporting the NIH to establish seven PHEOCs one at national level and six at state-level. Through a workshop held in July 2021, the NIH gained an understanding of what these operations centres are, how they function and their added value. With the skills acquired, the NIH at the national and state levels identified and selected qualified teams to work in the PHEOCs and enabled them to provide policy direction during outbreak response. The teams received training during two workshops in Kenya and Djibouti, during November and December 2021. Technical teams from WHO supported the FMOH with structural designs that could be adapted to construct or establish PHEOCs in Somalia, in addition to having procured and installed basic IT equipment for the centres in Galmudug, Jubaland, Puntland and Somaliland. WHO has also supported the development of the PHEOC manual, SOPs and costed operational plan, which will collectively guide daily operations at the centres and longer-term plans. WHO and PHAS will continue liaising with one another in relation to the establishment and operationalization of these PHEOCs.
Capacity-building for IHR (2005)
To equip the NIH with the capacity required to fulfil its mandate as the National Focal Point (NFP) for IHR 2005 in Somalia, several training events virtual and physical were organized for NIH staff and the IHR task force. These one-week trainings were conducted with the support experts from the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean in Cairo, Egypt, during October 2021, and helped to build substantial capacity of the NIH to perform its functions as the NFP for IHR (2005) in Somalia.
Strengthening health through digitalization: Data for action
Somalias health system has been weakened by decades of conflict and recurring natural disasters. In particular, Somalia lacks a comprehensive Health Information Management System (HIMS) capable of electronically collecting and sharing information from community to national level. While WHO (in collaboration with PHAS as well) continues to support establishing and implementing an IDSR strategy in Somalia, SPIDER Center, the FMOH and health authorities in Puntland, Galmudug and Banaadir launched a three-year project entitled Health Alliance for Digital Development and Action (HADDA). The aim of this project, funded by the Swedish International Development Agency (SIDA), is to create and strengthen a HIMS in Puntland, Galmudug and Banaadir as a pilot project, which will then inform further development and expansion of such systems at national level across Somalia. Overall, this collaboration will help strengthen Somalias health system, as well as how health data is stored, thereby improving health for all. In addition, a comprehensive assessment of the existing health information system in Somalia was been conducted by WHO from 8 to 15 September 2022, with the participation of SPIDER, in addition to a national policy dialogue and stakeholder consultation workshop from 5 to 7 December to develop a national health information system strategic plan. In this regard, WHO has spearheaded the Harmonized Health Facility Assessment (HHFA), also with financial support from Sweden. The HHFA is a comprehensive health facility survey that assesses the availability of health facility services and the capacities of facilities to provide services at required standards of quality. In these respects, for bettering health digitalization across Somalia in support of evidence-based decision making, WHO and SPIDER will continue to continue working together closely to offer one another technical support, as well as jointly work to identify of local opportunities for additional resource support targeting the digitalization of health.
Unexpected results
Besides the factual examples of results provided above, the collaboration between Sida and the WHO Somalia has resulted in a close dialogue, including joint efforts to strengthening health sector coordination, harmonization and alignment. This close dialogue has been helpful, in particular since the World Bank/GFF health project was approved in June 2021. Aid coordination in the health sector and beyond has been struggling over the last years and the entrance of the World Bank/GFF project has added to the complexity, hence also highlighting the importance of strong collaboration between UN agencies and like minded donors in the sector.
